extracted.intended_audience: design patent practitioners, patent litigators, and design patent owners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether an accused product infringes a U.S. design patent after Egyptian Goddess v. Swisa, focusing on the applicable legal tests, role of prior art, burdens of production, and evidentiary requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer test — sole test for determining design patent infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'ordinary observer' test ... is the 'sole test for determining whether a design patent has been infringed.' (adopts Gorham v. White standard from 1871).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this rule, infringement is assessed by whether an ordinary observer would view the patented design and the accused design as 'substantially the same.' The patentee bears the burden of proving that the two designs would appear substantially the same to the ordinary observer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial similarity requirement (Gorham)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requires substantial similarity between the patented design and the accused design when viewed by an ordinary observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the overall visual impression created by the patented design and accused design rather than dissecting into isolated elements. The inquiry centers on whether the ordinary observer, familiar with the prior art, would find the designs substantially the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of novelty test eliminated
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior 'point of novelty' test — which required identifying points of novelty in the patented design relative to the prior art — has been removed and is no longer required to prove design patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previously, patentee had to produce prior art designs and identify one or more points of novelty. That separate requirement no longer applies; courts will instead apply only the ordinary observer/substantial-similarity inquiry (while still considering prior art as described elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of prior art through the ordinary observer familiar with prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity under the ordinary observer test is to be considered from the perspective of an ordinary observer who is familiar with the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claimed and accused designs are not plainly dissimilar, resolution 'will benefit from a comparison of the claimed and accused designs with the prior art.' If there are many similar prior art designs, differences that seem minor 'in the abstract' can become significant to an observer conversant with that prior art. Thus prior art is used to inform what an ordinary observer would perceive as significant differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of production of prior art falls on the accused infringer
rubrics_metrics.description: A pro-patentee rule from the case: the burden of production of prior art designs will fall on the accused infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the eliminated point-of-novelty regime the patentee had to produce prior art; post-Egyptian Goddess, accused infringers should be prepared to produce prior art designs to show distinctions and influence the ordinary-observer comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: No verbal description of the diagrams required
rubrics_metrics.description: The court decided that a 'verbal description' of the diagrams is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations/diagrams of designs can be relied upon without a concomitant verbal description; parties and courts may focus on the visual comparison rather than requiring textual articulation of design elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to compare claimed and accused designs with prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: In some instances the designs will be sufficiently distinct that it is clear the patentee has not met its burden; in other instances, when not plainly dissimilar, comparison with the prior art will aid resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior-art comparisons especially where similarities are not obvious or where many prior art examples exist; determine whether differences that are subtle in isolation become significant in view of the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement determinations may turn on technical points of similarity rather than broad totality
rubrics_metrics.description: The court's application demonstrates proving infringement under the ordinary observer test can be difficult and 'many cases will likely turn on technical points of similarity between designs rather than simply a broader totality of similarity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be prepared to litigate or document fine-grained, technical visual distinctions between designs and not rely solely on overall gestalt arguments.
